hook: Two meadows each hold the same five kinds of wildflower. In one, every kind is common; in the other, clover covers almost everything. Counting species says they are equally diverse. Your eyes say they are not. Simpson's index, on the formula sheet, puts a number on the difference.

prereq.q: What two things does species diversity combine?
options: Number of trophic levels and energy flow
prereq.why: Diversity counts how many species there are (richness) and how evenly individuals are spread among them (relative abundance).

prereq.q: Which community is more likely to keep functioning if one species declines?
options: One with many species, evenly represented
One dominated by a single species
prereq.why: When individuals are spread among many species, the loss of one removes a smaller share of the community; diversity tends to support stability.

figure.caption: Same four species, same 20 plants. The even plot has D = 0.75; the plot dominated by one species has D = 0.27.

chain.cause: Each species makes up a fraction n/N of the community.
chain.effect: Squaring that fraction gives the chance that two individuals picked at random both belong to that species.

chain.cause: Adding the squares over all species…
chain.effect: …gives Σ(n/N)², the chance that two random individuals are the same species.
D = 1 − Σ(n/N)² is the chance that two random individuals are different species: higher D, more diversity.

chain.cause: One common species has a large n/N, and squaring makes it larger still compared with rare species.
chain.effect: Dominance by one species pulls D down sharply, while adding a rare species raises D only slightly.

ideas: D runs from 0 (one species) toward 1 (many species, evenly represented). Two equal species give 0.5.
Same richness can give very different D: five species at 20 each give 0.80; one at 80 and four at 5 give 0.35.
Forgetting the "1 −" is the classic slip: it reports similarity (0.65) instead of diversity (0.35).

misconception.wrong: Two communities with the same number of species have the same diversity.
misconception.right: Simpson's index also counts evenness. A community dominated by one species has a much lower index than one with the same species in equal numbers.

summary: Simpson's diversity index, D = 1 − Σ(n/N)², is the probability that two individuals chosen at random belong to different species. It runs from 0 (one species) toward 1, and it rises with both species richness and evenness. Dominance by one species lowers it sharply; a single rare new species barely changes it. Compare communities, or one community over time, by their D values and explain the change with richness, evenness and the biology behind them.
